hero.headline: Why can’t we just be friends?
hero.lead: Texans for a Safe Israel stands with the Jewish people in their God-given homeland — especially Jerusalem, Judea, and Samaria — and educates in Texas by building friendships without a hidden agenda.
hero.imageAlt: The TFSI lodge in Granbury with Texas and Israeli flags over the entrance

mission.title: A connector for the Jewish people
body: TFSI’s greatest role has been as a connector. Guests from the Biblical Heartland sit in a Texas house and tell their own story. Donors then fund the needs those friendships make visible: security, survivors, soldiers, and the next generation of visitors.

In Texas we educate through respectful relationships where real friendships can thrive. Most of the Christians who come through the house have never been to Israel and have never known a Jewish person. The guests change that.
mission.imageAlt: An Israeli flag hanging inside the log lodge in Granbury

work.title: The work
work.intro: Named people, named places, named items. These are the areas TFSI funds and the friendships behind them.

items.title: Critical needs
items.summary: When a community or family asks for help, TFSI moves quickly — drones, appliances, medical bags, or the specific item that keeps people safe.

items.title: Holocaust survivors
items.summary: Practical care without an agenda: appliances, home repairs, grocery cards at the holidays, and the things that restore dignity late in life.

items.title: Security and tactical supplies

items.title: Soldiers and families
items.summary: Food and drink for battalions in the field, and support for widows, orphans, and traumatized children through trusted Israeli partners.

items.title: Hosting and education

items.title: Influencer trips

quote.text: To Jews and to Christians we simply say: why can’t we just be friends?

closing.title: Stand with the people of the Heartland
closing.body: Every gift goes through Texans for a Safe Israel, a U.S. 501(c)(3). It keeps the house able to answer the next call from Arugot, Itamar, Shiloh, or a survivor in Texas.

hero.headline: What sets us apart
hero.lead: For more than a decade the house in Granbury has hosted the pioneers of Israel — most of them from Judea and Samaria. An interested group gathers. God’s covenant people tell the story of living out biblical prophecy in the land.
hero.imageAlt: An Israeli flag hanging inside the TFSI lodge

story.title: Friendships that fund the work
body: Those stories come with sacrifice, opposition, and immediate needs. That is the work: stand with the Jewish people, serve them, and take part in what is happening in the land.

President Ann Stacy has hosted Orthodox Jewish guests since October 2011. Texans for a Safe Israel was formed as a 501(c)(3) in 2018–2019 so those friendships could fund security projects and Holocaust education — not just conversation.
Mike Isley, founder of Texans for Israel, serves as vice president. The lodge flies Texas and Israeli flags over the same door for a reason.

story: There would be no Texans for a Safe Israel if not for this couple.

Ann met Jodi by phone in 2014, a few weeks before David Wilder arrived. In the days that followed, Jodi lost their son. Two weeks after that, doctors gave her a grim diagnosis. She never stopped working for Israel, Judea, Samaria, and the Jewish people.

Keith stayed behind the scenes and made sure the details were attended to. They led group trips to Israel and talked about their covenant friends and the promises of God. Jodi was mentor, cheerleader, and friend.
Keith later passed away. Jodi could not have done the work without him. He never gave up on one of the Stacy children.

story: Tova’s family survived the Holocaust. After liberation they walked back into their hometown. Their house was still standing and stripped of everything. Nothing was returned. The carpentry shop had no tools.

They immigrated to Israel in 1949 and lived in crowded immigrant housing with a communal kitchen. Tova remembers the dances held to welcome new residents — people hoping to find a relative, or news of one.
She will not walk across a floor without her shoes. In the Shoah, shoes were the difference between life and death. The children were never allowed to remove them.
Tova is a strong speaker and still teaches Hebrew. She lives in Arlington in the Dallas–Fort Worth area. Contact TFSI to be put in touch with her.

faq.a: No. This is not a tour operator. The team listens, recommends, and connects. You then work directly with the guides or hosts they introduce.

faq.q: Is there a cost for the consultation?
faq.a: No. The one-on-one planning session is free.

faq.q: Can I book a full-day or half-day itinerary?
faq.a: They will help design a visit — a few hours or a full day — and refer you to trusted guides or hosts who can run it.

faq.q: What kinds of visitors do you work with?
faq.a: Individuals, couples, families, small groups, first-timers, and returning visitors, including people with specific religious or cultural interests.

faq.q: Is it safe to visit Judea and Samaria?
faq.a: Travelers are referred to locations and providers that understand current security and travel guidelines. Safety and comfort are the first filter.

faq.q: Can you help with transportation or lodging?
faq.a: They do not book logistics directly. They will recommend transportation and lodging in or near the areas you will visit.

faq.q: Can I bring a group or community?
faq.a: Yes. Tell them the goal of the group and they will shape the visit around it.

faq.q: Is this a religious or political program?
faq.a: The point is the land through its people and stories — not slogans. The region is tied to biblical heritage and modern Zionism. Visitors from any background who will engage respectfully are welcome.

stories.title: What the money actually does
stories.lead: Named people, named places, named items. No invented totals.

items.title: Meeting critical needs
body: The Monday after the October 7 massacre, before Texas sunrise, TFSI called Jeremy Gimpel. His family and others live at Arugot Farm in the Judean Desert, surrounded by hostile neighbors. He needed a drone — the equivalent of fifty men on watch. The next day it was active. The farm later became a fortress for fifteen mothers and children while their fathers were at war.

items.title: Holocaust survivors
body: Survivors are often the group most wary of the word Christian. The work is kindness without proselytizing: two air conditioners, a refrigerator, washer and dryer, a deep freezer, iPads, phones, computers, a remodeled bathroom, a bread maker for challah, grocery cards at the holidays.
A 92-year-old concert pianist received a piano. If you want more on this work, contact the house and ask.

items.title: Security
body: Since October 7, TFSI has funded drones, bulletproof vests, scopes, cameras, helmets, medical bags, tactical boots, winter jackets, and a hand-warmer campaign. Communities helped include Har Bracha, Chavat Gilad, Arugot Farm, Susya, Itamar, Shiloh, and Homesh.

items.title: Feed the soldiers
body: Donations fed battalions in the field. Judy Tashbook Safern organized and raised most of those funds through tfsi.org — water, Coca-Cola, Red Bull, whatever they asked for.

items.title: Emotional needs
body: Amitsim, headed by Rabbi Yehuda and Hadass Glick, works with young widows and orphans. David Rubin’s Shiloh Israel Children’s Fund works with traumatized children. After October 7, that demand is not shrinking.

items.title: Israel trips
body: The first TFSI trip was May 2023: seven American Christians with nine American Jews from Americans for a Safe Israel. Contact the house for the next one.

items.title: The Biblical Highway
body: One long goal is that Route 60 become known as Israel’s national highway — the Biblical Highway. Rest stops in the Holy Cities, scenic overlooks, tourist information, a restaurant, a hotel. Tourism and Israeli business both change if people can actually travel the spine of the land.

items.title: Young adult influencers
body: Support for Israel is high among retired Americans and drops sharply in younger age groups. TFSI takes young people to the land. A page of those stories is still being built. Until then, the invitation is the same: come to Israel and become an influencer yourself.

items.title: Texas–Israel Embassy
body: A working embassy between the State of Texas and the State of Israel: staffers from Texas in Israel, staffers from Israel in Texas. A place Texans can go for assistance, guides, and recommended travel — and a place for Texas and Israeli businesses to meet.
